title: FT Graphics Standards — implementable spec for a UK property-price web app
rules: BACKGROUND — The FT tint is #FFF1E5 ('paper' in o-colors). It is a warm off-white: HSL 27.7deg, 100% saturation, 94.9% lightness. Against pure white it measures only 1.11:1, so it reads as 'not-white paper' rather than as a colour. Every chart surface, every card, and the page itself sits on it. Never render a chart on #FFFFFF and never render a white card on the tint — the tint IS the card.

BACKGROUND — Use #F2DFCE ('wheat') for an inset panel that must separate from the page, and #FFFCFA for the banded row highlights that sit behind ranked bars (this is the only background ornament FT permits inside a plot). Dark/social contexts use #333333; do not invent a dark grey.

BACKGROUND — Note the discrepancy in FT's own code: g-chartframe v5.3.3 hardcodes #FFF1E0 for all four web frames, while o-colors and g-chartcolour both specify #FFF1E5. #FFF1E5 is the canonical brand value; standardise on it and do not mix the two in one product.

GREY RAMP — Every FT grey is black mixed over the paper tint, not a neutral grey. This is the single most important structural fact in the system: it is why FT charts feel warm. Derived ramp (all corroborated against FT's shipped styles.css): 5% #F2E5DA, 10% #E6D9CE, 20% #CCC1B7, 30% #B3A9A0, 40% #999189, 60% #66605C, 70% #4D4845, 80% #33302E. Never substitute #CCCCCC, #999999, #666666 or any cool grey.

PALETTE ROLES — Primary series / 'now' / the subject: Oxford blue #0F5499 (6.90:1 on paper, passes AA as text as well as fill). Highlight / the one asset in focus: Claret #990F3D (7.62:1). Muted / 'then' / everything-else context: black-30 #B3A9A0 (2.08:1, fill only). Secondary series: Teal #0D7680 (4.84:1). Tertiary: Velvet #593380 (8.58:1).

PALETTE ROLES — Directional semantics: rise / positive = Jade #00994D, fall / negative = Crimson #CC0000. These are the two colours the FT retains in its stripped-back whitelabel palette alongside black and white, which is what marks them as the status pair. Both are fill-grade on paper (3.35:1 and 5.32:1) — Jade must never be used for small text.

PALETTE ROLES — Alert / regulatory pressure (EPC deadline, covenant breach): Mandarin #FF8833. At 2.15:1 on paper it is a fill-only colour. Any alert must also carry a text label; the colour alone is not the signal.

PALETTE ROLES — Multi-series categorical (4+ property types, boroughs, sectors) use FT's own web line palette in order: #0F5499, #EB5E8D, #70DCE6, #9DBF57, #208FCE, #7F062E, #C2B7AF, #CE3140. For bars use the FT bar palette in order: #1E558C, #94D2E6, #1E8FCC, #B3325D, #FF75A3, #D9CCC3, #AECC70, #F34D5B. Do not reorder them — the sequence alternates dark/light deliberately so adjacent series separate in greyscale.

PALETTE — Sequential (price per sq ft heat, density): #F3DEC8, #98C3CE, #649EC1, #3C78AE, #0F5499. Diverging (price change +/-, 5-step): #B31147, #D75D79, #CEC6B9, #5884D6, #105BA6. FT deliberately diverges claret-to-oxford rather than red-to-green; never build a red/green diverging scale.

ACCESSIBLE PAIRINGS — FT separates series by luminance, not hue. Verified safe pairs on paper: Oxford #0F5499 vs black-30 #B3A9A0 = 3.31:1 (the canonical then/now pair); Oxford #0F5499 vs black-20 #CCC1B7 = 4.32:1; Oxford #0F5499 vs Wasabi #96CC28 = 3.99:1. Verified UNSAFE adjacent pairs: Oxford #0F5499 vs Claret #990F3D = 1.10:1, Claret vs Teal = 1.57:1, Jade vs Crimson = 1.59:1. Those three vanish in greyscale and in deuteranopia — only use them when the marks are separated by direct labels and never adjacent.

ACCESSIBLE PAIRINGS — Text on fills: white on Oxford = 7.64:1, on Claret = 8.43:1, on Velvet = 9.50:1, on Crimson = 5.89:1, on Teal = 5.36:1 — all pass AA. White on Jade #00994D = 3.71:1, so use it only at 18px+/bold. Body text #33302E on paper = 11.83:1; axis/annotation text #4D4845 = 8.15:1; subtitle and source #66605C = 5.59:1 — all AA or better. Do not lighten source text below #66605C.

ACCESSIBLE PAIRINGS — o-colors throws a build error when a text/background pair fails WCAG 2.1 AA; mirror that discipline with a unit test over your token pairs. Treat any hex below 3:1 on paper as non-text, fill-only.

TYPOGRAPHY — The FT typeface for charts is MetricWeb (a humanist sans), regular weight 400. Chart text is never set in FT's serifs (FinancierDisplayWeb / FinancierTextWeb) — those are for editorial headlines and body copy, not graphics. Weight map: thin 100, light 300, regular 400, medium 500, semibold 600, bold 700, black 900.

TYPOGRAPHY — Practical web stack when MetricWeb is unlicensed: font-family: MetricWeb, Metric, 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif. Metric's closest freely-available substitute is Inter or Roboto; both carry the tall x-height and open apertures that make FT axis labels legible at 14px.

TYPOGRAPHY — Titles are weight 400, not bold. This is counter-intuitive and it is the fastest way to spot a fake FT chart: FT sets a 24-28px title in regular weight and lets size, not weight, carry the hierarchy. Title fill is pure #000000 — the only place pure black appears in a chart.
TYPOGRAPHY — Every SVG text node carries font-feature-settings: 'tnum' 1 so digits are tabular and columns of numbers align. This is in FT's shipped stylesheet and is non-optional for a price app.

TYPE SCALE — Axis label size, annotation size, direct-label size and legend size are all the SAME value (FT calls it 'rem' in the frame config): 14px at small, 16px at medium, 18px at large. Setting these independently is the second-fastest way to break the look.

LAYOUT — A 60px x 4px solid #000000 bar sits at the very top-left of the graphic, above the title. It is FT's chart signature. Reproduce it; it costs nothing and it does most of the work of looking like an FT chart.

LAYOUT — Title and subtitle are left-aligned to the GRAPHIC's left edge (x = 1px), not to the plot area's left edge. Axis tick labels then hang left of the plot inside the left margin. This deliberate misalignment — text flush left, plot indented — is the FT layout signature.

LAYOUT — Vertical order, top to bottom, no exceptions: black bar, title, subtitle, plot, x-axis labels, source block. Title baseline at y=32, subtitle baseline at y=64, plot top margin 100 (medium frame, 700x500). Never centre anything.

LAYOUT — Title states the finding, in sentence case, with no full stop and no chart-type name. Real FT examples: 'Waste generation rate'; 'German election 2017: AfD and FDP surge, fuelled by gains from Merkel's CDU and previously disengaged voters'. For property: 'Prime central London flats have not recovered their 2016 peak' — not 'Bar chart of London prices'.

LAYOUT — Subtitle carries the unit of measure and the period, nothing else. Real FT examples: 'kg per person per day, 2010'; 'Percentages refer to the share of valid votes cast*'. For property: "£'000 per dwelling, 2019-2026" or '£ per sq ft, Q2 2026'. The subtitle is where the currency symbol lives, which is what lets the axis run bare.

LAYOUT — Source block sits at the bottom, left-aligned to the same x=1 as the title, in #66605C at source size, as stacked lines in this order: (1) optional footnote prefixed with an asterisk that matches an asterisk in the subtitle or a category label; (2) 'Source: <Provider>' — or 'Sources: <A>; <B>' semicolon-separated for several; (3) 'FT graphic: <Name>' or, for third parties, 'Graphic: <Your firm>'. An optional fourth line carries the copyright in 14px italic. Verbatim FT example from their own template: '*Flows totalling less than 1 per cent of votes excluded | Source: Infratest dimap | Graphic: John Burn-Murdoch / @jburnmurdoch'.

LAYOUT — Data vintage goes in the SUBTITLE, not the source line. 'Source: HM Land Registry Price Paid Data' is correct; 'Source: HM Land Registry, data to June 2026' is not — that belongs in the subtitle.

CHART JUNK — There is no axis line. FT sets .domain { stroke-width: 0 } on both axes in every web frame and g-axis explicitly calls selectAll('.domain').remove(). The gridlines and the labels define the space; nothing is drawn around it.

CHART JUNK — Horizontal gridlines only, on the value axis, at #E6D9CE (black-10), 1px, drawn edge-to-edge across the plot, behind every mark. Category-axis tick marks, where present, are #CCC1B7 (black-20), 1px. Never draw vertical gridlines on a categorical axis.

CHART JUNK — The zero line is a gridline in a darker grey, not an axis. FT gives the tick at value 0 (or a nominated reference value) the class .baseline and strokes it #999189 (black-40), 1px, solid. Same geometry as a gridline, one step darker. This applies to the 2016-peak line, a target yield, or a portfolio average just as it does to zero.

CHART JUNK — Zero baseline rule, in FT's own words from the Visual Vocabulary: a bar/column chart 'must always start at 0 on the axis'. A lollipop 'does not have to start at zero (but preferable)'. A line chart of price levels may be truncated, but must then show a labelled non-zero baseline and state the range in the subtitle. Never truncate a bar.

CHART JUNK — Direct labelling replaces legends at three series or fewer: put the series name at the end of the line / above the bar group, set in the series' own colour at rem size. Only render a legend at four or more series or in small multiples; when you do, it goes horizontally above the plot at rem size in #4D4845 with rect/line/circle markers.

CHART JUNK — Annotations are 1px #66605C leader lines and paths with text at rem size in #4D4845. No arrowheads by default, no callout boxes, no shadows, no rounded pills. The leader line touches the datum; the text sits clear of the marks.

CHART JUNK — Mark geometry: bars have no stroke, no gradient, no rounded corners; lines are 3px with stroke-linecap: square, stroke-linejoin: round, fill: none. Banded row highlights behind ranked bars are #FFFCFA.

THEN VS NOW — FT has exactly two forms and you should implement both. (a) Slope chart, for 2-3 time points where rank change is the story. FT's own note: 'Good for showing changing data as long as the data can be simplified into 2 or 3 points without missing a key part of story' and 'Perfect for showing how ranks have changed over time'. (b) Dumbbell dot plot with a connector line, for a single before/after across many categories.

THEN VS NOW — Slope geometry per FT's template: no x-axis at all, only two labelled x positions; value axis right-aligned; left and right margins widened to 150px each to hold the labels; category name direct-labelled at the start with text-anchor 'end' and at the end with text-anchor 'start'. Never add a legend to a slope chart.

THEN VS NOW — Colour it with FT's 'muted-first' logic: 'then' in black-30 #B3A9A0, 'now' in Oxford #0F5499 — 3.31:1 apart and it survives greyscale. If a single asset is the subject, mute every other slope to #CCC1B7 and take the subject to Claret #990F3D. Encode direction with the mute/highlight pair, not with red-vs-green.

THEN VS NOW — Dumbbell settings from FT's dot-plot template: lines true, geometry circle, sort descending, banded rows true, labels shown on the first group only. The connector is the change; the two dots are the endpoints; the sort is by the 'now' value.

RANKED BAR — Horizontal bars, not columns. FT's own guidance: bars are 'good when the data are not time series and labels have long category names' — which is every London borough, every scheme name, every landlord. 'Standard bar charts display the ranks of values much more easily when sorted into order.'
RANKED BAR — Sort descending on the column of interest. Category labels sit left of the plot, right-aligned (text-anchor: end) in #4D4845 at rem size. Bars start at zero, always.

RANKED BAR — Two permitted treatments and you must pick one, never both: (i) keep the bottom value axis with #E6D9CE gridlines and bare divided numbers; or (ii) set numbers/showNumberLabels true, drop the value axis entirely, and direct-label every bar with its value in #66605C. FT's template documents this exactly: 'numbers — set to true to show values at the end of the bars and remove x-axis'.

RANKED BAR — Single hue for the whole set unless one bar is the subject; then take every other bar to #CCC1B7 and the subject to #0F5499 or #990F3D. Multi-hue ranked bars are a category error — rank is the encoding, not category. Negative values run left of the #999189 zero baseline.

NUMBER FORMAT — The core FT convention: strip the currency symbol from the axis. Divide every tick by a divisor, format the result bare, and declare the unit once in the subtitle. divisor 1,000 -> subtitle "£'000"; divisor 1,000,000 -> subtitle '£mn'; divisor 1,000,000,000 -> subtitle '£bn'. An axis reading 0 200 400 600 800 under a subtitle reading "£'000 per dwelling" is correct FT; an axis reading £200,000 £400,000 is not.

NUMBER FORMAT — Integer ticks use a comma group separator (d3.format(',')). The moment any tick in the divided domain is non-integer, FT latches decimal formatting across the WHOLE axis so precision never goes ragged: span >= 0.5 -> 1dp, < 0.5 -> 2dp, <= 0.011 -> 3dp, < 0.0011 -> 4dp, < 0.00011 -> 5dp, < 0.000011 -> 6dp. Implement the latch, not just the format.

NUMBER FORMAT — In annotations, tooltips, prose and table cells the symbol returns and FT's magnitude abbreviations apply: '£450,000', '£1.2mn', '£3.4bn', '£1.1tn'. Lowercase, closed up to the numeral, no space. Use 'mn' not 'm' — the FT switched deliberately in February 2022 because screen readers read a bare 'm' as 'metres'. Below £1mn, write property prices out in full with commas: '£950,000', never '£0.95mn'.

NUMBER FORMAT — Percentages: '%' is fine in axis ticks and tight annotations; spell it 'per cent' as two words in prose and in source-line footnotes, per FT house style (their own template footnote reads 'less than 1 per cent of votes'). Rates: '5.25%' for a yield, '£42.50 per sq ft' in prose with '£ per sq ft' as the subtitle unit. Never mix magnitudes on a single axis.

NUMBER FORMAT — Dates: full four-digit years on large frames, abbreviated on small (FT's fullYear flag is true only on the 1180px frame). Match the repository's date convention elsewhere: 15 December 2025.
antiPatterns: White (#FFFFFF) chart backgrounds, or white cards floating on the #FFF1E5 tint. The tint is the surface.
Neutral greys — #CCCCCC, #999999, #666666, Tailwind's gray-500. Every FT grey is black mixed over paper and carries a warm cast; a cool grey next to #FFF1E5 reads as dirty.
Bold chart titles. FT titles are weight 400. Bold is the single clearest tell of a counterfeit FT chart.
Titles that name the chart type ('Bar chart of London prices') or restate the axis. The title states the finding.
Putting '£' on every axis tick. The unit is declared once in the subtitle and the axis runs bare.
'£1.2m', '£1.2M', '£1.2MM' or '£1,200k'. FT uses 'mn' for accessibility reasons; the others are wrong or ambiguous.
Truncating a bar chart's value axis. Bars must start at zero without exception.
Drawing an axis domain line, a box around the plot, or outward-pointing tick marks on the value axis.
Vertical gridlines on a categorical axis, or gridlines drawn over the top of the marks rather than behind them.
Legends on charts with three or fewer series. Direct-label at the end of the line or above the bar group in the series colour.
Multi-coloured ranked bars. Rank is the encoding; use one hue and highlight at most one bar.
Pairing Oxford #0F5499 with Claret #990F3D as two adjacent categorical series — they measure 1.10:1 against each other and are indistinguishable in greyscale and in deuteranopia.
Red/green for rise and fall as the sole encoding (Jade vs Crimson is 1.59:1). Encode direction with the muted/highlight pair or with position, and let colour reinforce rather than carry it.
Setting axis label, annotation and legend sizes independently. They are one value: 14/16/18px by frame size.
Proportional (non-tabular) figures. Without font-feature-settings: 'tnum' the digit columns in a price table will not align.
Centred titles, centred subtitles, or aligning the title to the plot's left edge rather than the graphic's left edge.
Rounded bar corners, gradient fills, drop shadows, 3D effects, glow, or animated entry transitions on the marks.
Putting the data vintage in the source line. Vintage belongs in the subtitle; the source line names the provider.
Reusing the FT masthead, the FT logo watermark, or the 'FT graphic:' credit line on work that is not the FT's. Use 'Graphic: Teddy James Advisory'.
Mixing #FFF1E0 (g-chartframe's hardcoded value) and #FFF1E5 (canonical) in the same product — the seam is visible where a chart meets the page.

BLOCKED / NOT REACHED: ft.com, ig.ft.com and registry.origami.ft.com are all blocked to this agent, so I could not inspect a rendered FT graphics page or the Origami registry docs. I did successfully curl the live production stylesheet at ig.ft.com/visual-vocabulary/styles.css and confirmed it matches the repo exactly, so the CSS values are production-verified. The Origami build service returned a 404 HTML error page rather than compiled CSS, so the custom-property values were derived from Sass source instead.

DERIVED, NOT COPIED — one genuine finding worth flagging. Every grey in FT's shipped chart CSS is black mixed over the paper tint at a fixed percentage. I verified this by computing the mix and matching it against the values FT actually ships: 10% -> #E6D9CE (their y-gridline), 20% -> #CCC1B7 (their x-axis line), 30% -> #B3A9A0 (their muted-first series colour), 40% -> #999189 (their baseline), 60% -> #66605C (their subtitle/source), 70% -> #4D4845 (their axis text), 80% -> #33302E (o-colors body text). All seven match exactly. The 50% and 90% steps in the token block are computed rather than observed and sit on a rounding boundary — treat them as lower-confidence.

DISCREPANCIES IN FT'S OWN CODE, resolved in the spec: (a) g-chartframe hardcodes the background as #FFF1E0 across all four web frames, while o-colors and g-chartcolour both say #FFF1E5 — I have standardised on #FFF1E5 as the canonical brand value and flagged the seam. (b) o-colors defines the 'muted' text use-case as black-20 (#CCC1B7), which measures only 1.60:1 on paper and fails WCAG badly; the FT graphics team does not use it for chart text. I have deliberately NOT propagated it and have used the graphics team's shipped values instead (#4D4845 axis, #66605C subtitle/source).

ALL CONTRAST RATIOS in the spec were computed here against WCAG 2.1 relative luminance, not recalled. The Oxford-vs-Claret 1.10:1 result is the most actionable: those are FT's two signature colours and they are almost perfectly matched in luminance, so a chart that uses them as adjacent categorical series is unreadable in greyscale and in deuteranopia. FT's own palettes avoid this by alternating dark and light down the sequence.

LICENSING: the FT publishes chart-doctor, visual-vocabulary-templates, g-chartcolour, g-chartframe and g-axis under MIT, but their README is explicit that "the MIT licence includes only the software, and does not cover any FT content made available using the software, which is copyright (c) The Financial Times Limited". The colour values, layout geometry and code patterns are safe to adopt. Do not reproduce the FT masthead or watermark, and credit the graphic as "Graphic: Teddy James Advisory" rather than "FT graphic:".
